content: In adolescents with type 1 diabetes, insulin resistance is believed to contribute to the worsening of metabolic control. To address this, the addition of metformin to insulin therapy has been explored as a means to improve insulin sensitivity. However, the available research on this topic is limited, consisting of only a few small trials or uncontrolled studies of short duration. To date, no systematic reviews have been conducted to summarize the evidence regarding the use of metformin in combination with insulin therapy for adolescents with type 1 diabetes. The objective of this investigation was to evaluate the effects of adding metformin to insulin therapy in adolescents with type 1 diabetes. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Additional searches were performed in databases of ongoing trials, reference lists of relevant reviews, and through direct contact with experts, authors, and manufacturers. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) lasting at least three months that compared metformin plus insulin therapy to insulin therapy alone in adolescents with type 1 diabetes. Cross-over trials and quasi-randomized controlled trials were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the abstracts, evaluated the quality of the studies, and extracted data. Authors of the studies were contacted to obtain any missing information. Only two trials, involving a total of 60 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These trials investigated the effects of adding metformin to insulin therapy over a three-month period in adolescents with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes. Due to differences in the clinical and methodological aspects of the studies, a meta-analysis could not be performed. Both studies indicated that metformin treatment reduced glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in adolescents with poor metabolic control. However, neither study demonstrated improvements in insulin sensitivity, body composition, or serum lipid profiles. One of the studies did report a 10% reduction in insulin dosage. Adverse effects were primarily gastrointestinal in nature, and one study also reported cases of hypoglycemia. No data were available regarding health-related quality of life, all-cause mortality, or morbidity. In conclusion, there is some evidence to suggest that adding metformin to insulin therapy may improve metabolic control in adolescents with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes. However, stronger evidence is needed from larger, longer-term studies to better understand the effects of this intervention on metabolic control, health-related quality of life, morbidity, and mortality in this patient population.
